1. The core ideas › Course conventions (use these exactly)
All AC magnitudes are rms. Mains “240 V” means V_rms = 240 V and V_pk = sqrt2 × 240 = 339.4 V.
1. The core ideas › Course conventions (use these exactly)
The voltage is the phase reference: V_1 = V_1∠ 0^°, I_1 = I_1∠φ.
1. The core ideas › Course conventions (use these exactly)
φ is the angle of the current relative to the voltage. Lagging (inductive) means φ < 0. Leading (capacitive) means φ > 0.
1. The core ideas › Course conventions (use these exactly)
The power triangle angle is -φ, so Q = V_1 I_1 sin(-φ). This is why an inductive load (with φ<0 ) gives Q>0.
1. The core ideas › Course conventions (use these exactly)
Always quote the power factor with its label, e.g. “0.8184 lag”.
1. The core ideas › Course conventions (use these exactly)
A real source or load is replaced by ideal elements you can analyse. For a DC source (a battery or power supply), the model is an EMF E in series with an internal resistance R_S.
Open circuit ( I = 0 ) the EMF E = V_oc
Loaded, with V and I measured the internal resistance R_S = (E - V)/I
Short circuit the internal resistance R_S = E/I_sc
Any load the terminal voltage V = E - I R_S
Maximum power occurs when R_L = R_S P_max = E^2/(4R_S), at 50 % efficiency
Trap: the power delivered to the load is VI (using the terminal voltage), not EI. EI is the total, and it includes the I^2R_S loss.
P_M = τω, ω = (2π n)/(60) rad/s (with n in rpm), τ = Fr, F = mg

P = V_1 I_1cosφ is the average of p(t). Its maximum is P + S and its minimum is P - S, where S = V_1I_1. The minimum is negative whenever Q ≠ 0 : energy then flows back to the source for part of each cycle.

To get a phase shift from a time delay: |φ| = (Δ t)/(T)× 360^°. If the current peaks earlier than the voltage, it is leading.
1. The core ideas › Single-phase AC power (Section 1.5)

1. The core ideas › Complex power and the power triangle (Section 2.4)
P and Q are each conserved. The total P is the sum of the element P ’s, and the same holds for Q. S is not: never add apparent powers. Add the P ’s, add the Q ’s, and then recombine.
1. The core ideas › Complex power and the power triangle (Section 2.4)

2. The method › Playbook D: finding R and X from measurements (Section 2.6)
Series: R = P/I^2 and X = Q/I^2. Parallel: R = V^2/P and X = V^2/Q.
2. The method › Playbook D: finding R and X from measurements (Section 2.6)
If asked, L = X/ω or C = 1/(ω|X|).
2. The method › Playbook D: finding R and X from measurements (Section 2.6)
If given two voltages in a series RL: V_L = √(V_1^2 - V_R^2) and φ = -arccos(V_R/V_1).
2. The method › Playbook D: finding R and X from measurements (Section 2.6)
List the P and Q of every load, with signs. For a motor given P and pf: S = P/pf and Q = Ptan(arccos pf), positive for lag.
2. The method › Playbook E: power triangle
P_tot = Σ P and Q_tot = Σ Q.
2. The method › Playbook E: power triangle
S_tot = √(P_tot^2 + Q_tot^2), pf = P_tot/S_tot, and the label comes from the sign of Q_tot.
2. The method › Playbook E: power triangle
Supply current: I = S/V for 1ph, or I_L = S/(sqrt3 V_L) for 3ph. Its angle is φ = -arctan(Q/P).
2. The method › Playbook E: power triangle
Sketch the triangle: P horizontal, Q vertical (up for positive), S as the hypotenuse, and -φ at the origin.

Open circuit. Majority carriers diffuse across the junction and recombine. This leaves fixed ionised dopants: + ions on the n side and − ions on the p side. That is the depletion region. Its field sets up the barrier V_0, which opposes further diffusion and drives the minority-carrier drift current I_S. At equilibrium I_D=I_S, so there is no net current.

E. System properties (do them in this order)
Static? Look for any index other than n, or any output memory.
Linear? First test x=0. If y≠0, it is nonlinear. Next look for nonlinear functions of x or y. If neither appears, it is linear. Gains that depend on n are fine.
Time-invariant? Use two columns. (i) Replace x(·) by x(·-d) and leave the explicit n alone. (ii) Replace every n by n-d. If they are equal, it is TI.
Causal? Check every n, including negative n, for a future input.
Stable? Bound the output in terms of M_x, or find one bounded input that blows up the output ( u(n) is the usual choice).

Direct substitution for y(n)=x(2-n) : y(-2)=x(4)=-1, y(-1)=x(3)=0, y(0)=x(2)=1, y(1)=2, y(2)=3, y(3)=x(-1)=4. So y(n)=-1,0,undersetuparrow1,2,3,4, starting at n=-2. As a check with the lecture order: shift left by 2 to get x(n+2), then reverse.

Example 3 — Properties with counterexamples (exam style, in the spirit of T2 Q1). Given y(n)=x(n)+x(-n). Classify it.
Dynamic. y(1)=x(1)+x(-1) needs an input from another time.
Time-varying. Delaying the input gives x(n-d)+x(-n-d). Delaying the output gives y(n-d)=x(n-d)+x(-n+d). These differ. Concrete case: with x=δ(n), y=2δ(n). With x=δ(n-1), y=δ(n-1)+δ(n+1)≠ 2δ(n-1).
Not causal. y(-1)=x(-1)+x(1) uses a future input.

By even symmetry, r_xx(l)=-1,0,undersetuparrow6,0,-1 for l=-2,…,2.

Reconstructing y(t) before reducing ω into (-π,π]. You just get x(t) back and lose the aliasing marks.

Missing the arrow. Every sequence answer must mark n=0 or list the indices. Applying x(α n+β) in the wrong order: scaling first, then shifting by β instead of β/α.
Calling cos(0.2π)x[n] time-varying. It is a constant gain. Only cos(0.2π n) would vary with time.

2. The method › Type D: diode circuits, the four-step assume-and-verify method (WS3 Q7, Q8, Q15–17, practice test Q3)

Verify. ON needs i_d > 0. OFF needs v_d < V_D (or v_d < 0 for the ideal model). If any check fails, flip that diode (usually the one with the most negative current) and go back to step 3. Repeat until every check passes. Then, and only then, compute V_o.

Not writing down the check, or checking the wrong quantity. ON needs a current check. OFF needs a voltage check. A correct V_o with no verification loses the verification marks.
Getting the sign of v_d wrong for an OFF diode. It is always V_anode - V_cathode. An OFF branch carries no current, so its resistors drop 0 V but its batteries still count.
Temperature direction. V_D falls by 2.5 mV/°C, while I_S doubles every 10 °C. With a 20 °C rise that is a factor of 4, not 2.

LCCDE (L04 slide 4). Σ_p=0^k a_p y(n-p) = Σ_q=0^m b_q x(n-q) with a_0 = 1. The order is k, the largest delay on the y side.
Idea Formula When you use it Trap
Characteristic equation λ^k + a_1λ^k-1 + … + a_k = 0 “Find the modes” Use the y coefficients only. The x side never affects the modes.
Distinct roots y_h(n) = C_1λ_1^n + C_2λ_2^n Real roots, λ_1 ≠ λ_2 Write 2^-n, not 2^n, for λ = 12.
Repeated root C_1λ^n + C_2 nλ^n Double root Two copies of λ^n give one unknown, not two. For λ = 1 the modes are 1 and n (T3 Q5c).
Complex pair re^± jθ r^n(Acosθ n + Bsinθ n) Discriminant < 0 Find r = |λ| and θ = ∠λ. The real form avoids complex constants.
No y(n-k) terms No modes (FIR) T3 Q2(a) The answer is “the modes are zero / there are none”. Say it outright.
Particular solution Use the same form as x(n) : Ka^n, K, K_1cos + K_2sin Non-homogeneous LCCDE with a functional-form input If a is a characteristic root, use Kna^n.
Total solution y(n) = y_h(n) + y_p(n), constants from y(0), …, y(k-1) “Find the output” Get y(0), y(1) by recursion using the given ICs. Never put y(-1) into the closed form.
Recursive form (slide 13) y(n) = -Σ_k=1^N a_k y(n-k) + Σ_k=0^M b_k x(n-k) “Using recursion, evaluate…” Move the y terms to the right and flip their signs.
Impulse response h(n) = output for x = δ with zero ICs “Find h(n) ” FIR: h(n) = b_n. IIR: modes plus recursion. If m ≥ k, add δ terms.
Convolution sum (slide 9) y(n) = Σ_k x(k)h(n-k) = Σ_k h(k)x(n-k) Output for any input Put the step limits into the sum before you sum anything.
Geometric sum. This is the workhorse for closed forms: Σ_k=k_1^k_2 r^k = (r^k_1 - r^k_2+1)/(1-r) (r ≠ 1), Σ_k=k_1^k_2 1 = k_2 - k_1 + 1.

Causal exponentials. Both steps on means k ≥ 0 and n-k ≥ 0, so the sum runs over 0 ≤ k ≤ n and is zero for n < 0. The result: a^n u(n) * b^n u(n) = (a^n+1 - b^n+1)/(a-b) u(n) (a ≠ b), a^n u(n) * a^n u(n) = (n+1)a^n u(n).
Property Test on h(n) LCCDE shortcut
Static h(n) = Kδ(n) Only an x(n) term
Causal h(n) = 0 for n < 0 No x(n+1) terms, initially at rest
Stable (BIBO) Σ_k |h(k)| < ∞ All |λ_i| < 1 (causal IIR). FIR is always stable.
FIR / IIR Finite / infinite number of nonzero samples No feedback means FIR. Any y(n-k) term means IIR in practice.

Interconnections (Video 2.6, T2 Q4). Cascade: h = h_1 * h_2, and the order does not matter. Parallel: h = h_1 + h_2, with a minus sign for a subtracting junction. Useful identities: x(n) * δ(n-d) = x(n-d) and x(n) * u(n) = Σ_k=-∞^n x(k).

Modes from the wrong side. The x coefficients ( b_q ) never enter the characteristic equation. A system with no y(n-k) terms has no modes. Don’t write “ λ = 0, modes 0^n ” and leave it unexplained.
Sign flip in recursion. y(n) - y(n-1) + y(n-2) becomes y(n) = +y(n-1) - y(n-2) + …. One sign error ruins every sample after it.
Plugging y(-1) into the closed form. The closed form is only valid for n ≥ 0. Always get y(0) and y(1) by recursion first. T3 Q4 shows why: y[0] = 1 - (-1) - 14(2) = 1.5.
Repeated roots. Writing C_1(-12)^n + C_2(-12)^n leaves you one equation short. You need nλ^n. Also watch the course’s notation: (-12)^n is written as (-2)^-n.
Forgetting the δ terms when m ≥ k. For y(n) - 0.5y(n-1) = x(n) - x(n-1), the mode form fits only from n = 1 (see New Q3).
Dropping step limits. Σ_k=0^n only exists for n ≥ 0, so the answer needs u(n). Finite pulses need separate cases for n. A closed form with no range stated is incomplete.
Geometric sum off by one. Σ_k=0^n r^k has n+1 terms, so the numerator is 1 - r^n+1, not 1 - r^n. If a = b, the formula (a^n+1 - b^n+1)/(a-b) becomes 0/0. Use (n+1)a^n instead.
“Stable” for |λ| = 1. u(n), (n+1)u(n) and cos(ω_0 n)u(n) are all not absolutely summable, so these systems are unstable.

SC/OC formulas swapped. The OC test is parallel ( V^2/P, V^2/Q ). The SC test is series ( P/I^2, Q/I^2 ). If your R_C comes out at 0.6 Ω, you have swapped them.
Using V/I for X. In the SC test V/I = |Z|, not X. In the OC test V/I is the parallel combination, not X_M. You need Q from √(S^2-P^2).
Forgetting the per-phase conversion for a star 3-phase test: V_L/sqrt3 and P/3. Getting it wrong puts R out by a factor of 3 and X by a factor of sqrt3 or 3.
Not referring secondary parameters. Practice 3.27 says “secondary parameters are NOT referred”. R_2' = n^2R_2, not nR_2.
OC test done on the LV side. The resulting R_C, X_M are referred to the LV side. Multiply by n^2 before putting them on an HV-primary circuit.
Putting R_C and X_M into the KVL. In the simplified circuit they hang across V_1. They carry no I_2' and do not affect V_2'.
Wrong sign on the current angle. Lagging pf (load absorbs Q) means φ < 0. A load “generating” Q is leading, so φ > 0 (2024 test Q7).
“Capacitive load makes V_2' lead”. A capacitive load raises |V_2'|, but V_2' still lags V_1 for any normal load (see New Question 4). Don’t confuse a magnitude rise with a phase lead.

Open-circuit (OC) behaviour. With I_2' = 0 the input sees only R_C ∥ jX_M. Then I_1 = V_1/(R_C ∥ jX_M), P = 3V_1^2/R_C and Q = 3V_1^2/X_M. With the model’s constant R_C and X_M, halving V gives: current × 0.5, P × 0.25, Q × 0.25, pf × 1.

Why the OC current is not zero. The core has finite permeability, so it needs an mmf (the magnetising current through X_M ) to set up the flux. The core also has hysteresis and eddy-current losses, and these need a real current (through R_C ). Saturation makes the magnetising current rise much faster than the voltage near rated flux. Using R + jX in the OC calculation. On open circuit no current flows in the series branch, so use only R_C ∥ jX_M.

An NPN is n (emitter, heavily doped) / p (base, thin and lightly doped) / n (collector). A PNP is the reverse. There are two junctions: emitter–base (EBJ) and collector–base (CBJ).
1. The core ideas › 1.1 Physics in five lines (enough for the MCQs)

In active mode the forward-biased EBJ injects electrons into the base. The base is thin and lightly doped, so few of them recombine (about 1 %). Most of them diffuse across and are swept into the collector by the reverse-biased CBJ. Diffusion dominates at the EBJ and drift at the CBJ (Lecture 3). This is Practice Test Q1 IV, answer (a).

Using β I_B without the (β+1)R_E term. In any circuit with an emitter resistor, the base loop contains (β+1)R_E, not R_E and not β R_E. Leaving it out typically makes I_B come out 3–5 times too big.
Skipping the β R_E≥10R_2 statement. WS5 Q7 fails the test. Using the approximation there gives I_C 16 % high. Write the test explicitly every time.
Mixing up V_C and V_CE. These are equal only when the emitter is grounded. With R_E present, V_C=V_CE+V_E. Practice Test Q7 asks for V_C.
Getting I_C,sat wrong with R_E present. It is V_CC/(R_C+R_E), not V_CC/R_C.
Using the WS4 handout’s mode table. Its saturation and cut-off rows are swapped. Saturation is forward/forward and cut-off is reverse/reverse.
Reading “β at the Q-point” as the curve spacing. It means β_dc=I_CQ/I_BQ at that point. Δ I_C/Δ I_B between neighbouring curves is β_ac, which is a different, slightly smaller number on the Q6 graph.
Not showing your graph readings. In Q6, write “read I_CQ≈4.5 mA, V_CEQ≈8.0 V” before you divide. The marks are for the readings and the method.
Treating a negative V_CE as an arithmetic slip. It means the transistor is saturated (New question 5 shows this).

DC: the no-load speed is proportional to V. The speed drop n_NL - n_R stays constant when V changes, so the curve slides sideways and keeps its slope. Lecture example: 1000/850 rpm at V_R becomes 500/350 rpm at 0.5V_R.

AC (induction and synchronous): n_S is proportional to f. You must change V in proportion (V/f constant). The back-emf equation E = 4.44NfhatΦ shows that, ignoring stator resistance, hatΦ ∝ V/f. If you cut f without cutting V, the flux rises, the core saturates and the current becomes very large. The slip speed at rated torque ( n_S - n_R ) stays constant.
Trap: for an induction machine, do not scale n_R in proportion. 1500/1400 rpm at 50 Hz becomes 500/400 rpm at 16.67 Hz, not 500/466.7 rpm.

p vs poles. The course formula n_S = 60f/p uses pole-pairs. “6-pole, 50 Hz” gives 1000 rpm, not 500 rpm.

Rounding p to the nearest integer instead of down. For an induction motor, n_S must be above n_R. (Rounding to the nearest happens to work for PQ 4.11, which asks for the closest n_S to a desired speed. That is a different question.)
rpm in E = kω. Always use rad/s. k = 220/1500 is wrong; k = 220/(2π · 1500/60) = 1.4 V/(rad/s) is right (PQ 5.3a).
Scaling the rated speed in proportion when you change V or f. It is the speed drop (DC) or slip speed (IM) that stays constant.
Changing f without changing V on an AC machine. This saturates the core and causes overcurrent. Jun24 Q3a(ii) asks for “safe” operation, and the marks are for “halve V and f”.
Assuming part-load power = fraction × rated power on a DC or induction machine. The speed rises, so P/P_R = x n/n_R.
Using P_in = EI. Input power is VI. EI is the converted (output) power.
Sign errors for generators. With I flowing out, E = V + IR. Generator efficiency is V/E, not E/V.

Zero on the unit circle at angle ω_0 lvert H(ω_0)rvert = 0 exactly (a null, used for notch filters)

Playbook B: steady-state output to a sum of sinusoids
List every input component with its frequency ω_i, amplitude A_i and phase φ_i. A constant C is ω = 0. (-1)^n = cos(π n) is ω = π. Keep sin as sin.
Evaluate H(ω_i) for each component as a complex number, then convert to |H(ω_i)| and θ(ω_i). Use exact values ( π/3, not 1.047) until the end.
Write each output term as A_i|H(ω_i)|cos(ω_i n + φ_i + θ(ω_i)).
Drop any term with |H(ω_i)| = 0 and say so (“blocked by the zero at e^jω_i ”).
Add the terms (superposition is allowed because the system is linear). DC terms: C · H(0), and H(0) is real.
For an IIR system, say it is the steady-state response: the stable poles’ transients have died out.
Playbook C: identify H(ω) from input-output data

If the input is a single complex exponential or sinusoid at ω_0, you get only H(ω_0) = (output complex amplitude) / (input complex amplitude). State that H at other frequencies cannot be found (T4 Q3b).
If the input is a general signal (exponential, finite sequence): H(ω) = Y(ω)/X(ω) using DTFT pairs.
If the input is δ(n) (check whether something like u(n) - u(n-1) is really δ(n) ), then the output is h(n). DTFT it.
With several sinusoid pairs and a known filter form (for example b_0 + b_1e^-jω ), set up one equation per frequency and solve for the coefficients.
Substitute x(n) = Acos(ω_0 n) into the system equation.
Use trig identities: cos^2α = 12 + 12cos 2α, cosαcosβ = 12[cos(α-β) + cos(α+β)], and cos(π n) = (-1)^n.
Reduce every frequency into [0, π]. Use cos(ω n) = cos((2π - ω)n), so 5π/4 → 3π/4.

If any output frequency is not in the input, the system is not LTI. Name the cause: a squared, product or constant term means nonlinear; a time-dependent coefficient or time-scaling means time-varying.
If no new frequency appears, you cannot conclude it is LTI from this test alone.
Playbook E: geometric evaluation and sketching
Mark the poles (×) and zeros (○). Ignore those at the origin for magnitude.
Walk e^jω from ω = 0 (the point z = 1 ) anticlockwise to ω = π (the point z = -1 ).
Check the key points: ω = 0, π, and the angle of every pole and zero near the circle. At each point estimate prod V_k / prod U_k.
Draw the sketch: zero on the circle means touching 0; pole near the circle means a peak, sharper the closer it is. Between features, draw a smooth curve.
For a value, compute each vector length exactly with |e^jω - q| = √((cosω - Req)^2 + (sinω - Imq)^2). Multiply by |b_0|.
For phase, add the angles of the zero vectors, subtract the angles of the pole vectors, and add ω(N-M) + ∠ b_0. Watch for the ±π jump when e^jω passes through a zero on the circle.

A negative “magnitude”. 2cos(2ω) at ω = π/3 is -1. The magnitude is 1 and the phase gains +π, giving -2π/3 + π = π/3 in T4 Q4. Writing an amplitude of -1 with phase -2π/3 is equivalent, but a “magnitude response” sketch must be ≥ 0.
Wrong signs on the a_k. Read the denominator from the equation with all y terms on the left: y(n) - 0.5y(n-1) → 1 - 0.5e^-jω.
Forgetting the DC and (-1)^n terms. A constant is a sinusoid at ω = 0 and is multiplied by H(0). Using H = 1 for DC is wrong unless H(0) = 1. (-1)^n is ω = π.
Claiming H(ω) from one sinusoid pair. One pair gives one value H(ω_0) only (T4 Q3b).
“No new frequencies, so it is LTI”. That doesn’t follow. The test only proves non-LTI. y(n) = x(-n) and y(n) = x(n) + 1 (which only adds DC) are both non-LTI.
Counting origin poles/zeros in |H|. They have unit distance to the circle and don’t affect magnitude. They do affect phase through ω(N-M).
Reversing the vectors. Use e^jω - z_k (from the zero to the circle point), not z_k - e^jω. Reversing them adds 180^° per factor.
Leaving frequencies above π. Reduce them: 5π/4 ≡ 3π/4 for a real cosine (T4 Q5c).

The active-mode base loop for any single-transistor bias circuit has this form:
I_B = (V_Th - V_BE)/(R_Th + (β+1)R_E), I_C = β I_B = (β (V_Th - V_BE))/(R_Th + (β+1)R_E)
If (β+1)R_E R_Th, then I_C ≈ (V_Th-V_BE)/R_E, which does not depend on β. This is why emitter and voltage-divider bias are stable.
If R_E = 0 (fixed bias), I_C ∝ β. Doubling β doubles I_C.

Worst cases. β_max gives the largest I_C and the smallest V_CE, so check it to avoid saturation. β_min gives the smallest I_C, so check it to guarantee saturation (WS5 Q12, Q13) or to guarantee a minimum current.

Concentric-circle method. Write x_1(m) anticlockwise on the outer circle. Write x_2(m) clockwise (that is the reversal) on the inner circle, with x_2(0) aligned with x_1(0). Multiply aligned pairs and add to get y(0). Rotate the inner circle one step anticlockwise and repeat for y(1), and so on. It is the same arithmetic as the matrix rows.
Wrap shortcut (often fastest): compute the linear convolution y_lin(n) (length L+M-1 ), then fold every sample at index ≥ N back by N and add. This is time aliasing again: y_N(n)=Σ_m y_lin(n+mN).

Using W_N=e^+j2π/N in the forward DFT, or forgetting 1/N and the sign flip in the IDFT.
Reversing a sequence as x_3,x_2,x_1,x_0 instead of the circular reversal x_0,x_3,x_2,x_1. This breaks both the time-reversal property and the circulant matrix.
Computing linear convolution when circular was asked (or the reverse). A circular answer always has exactly N samples.
Choosing N=max(L,M) or N=L+M for linear convolution via DFT. The condition is N≥ L+M-1.
Saying zero padding “improves resolution” in the sense of separating close frequencies. It only samples X(ω) more densely (true resolution is for pack D6).
Forgetting X(k)=Nc_k when converting between DFT and DFS.
Circular shift: using e^+j2π kl/N for a delay. A delay of l multiplies by e^-j2π kl/N.
Deconvolution: dividing by H(k)=0 without comment.

1. The core ideas › 1.8 Two short-answer explanations

At no load the rotor runs at nearly synchronous speed, so the rotor current is almost zero. The stator still has to set up the rotating airgap flux. That needs magnetising current in X_M. An induction machine has an airgap, so it needs much more magnetising current than a transformer. The no-load current is typically 25–60 % of rated current (Lecture 7.8.5).

The trap is rounding. N always rounds up, because a larger N gives a finer resolution. After rounding, the actual resolution F_s/N is better than required. Use the minimum F_s unless told otherwise, because a higher F_s needs a larger N for the same resolution.
1. The core ideas › 1.2 Choosing F_s, N and T_0
Zero-padding L samples to length N > L samples the same DTFT X(ω) at more points ( 2π/N apart instead of 2π/L ).
It gives a smoother picture and a better estimate of where a peak is. This is interpolation.
It adds no new information about the signal. Two tones closer than 1/T_0 stay merged, whatever N is.

Slide 9 says zero-padding gives “better resolution for sampled DTFT”. That means a finer frequency grid. It does not mean better ability to separate tones. In an exam, keep the two words apart: write “bin spacing” for F_s/N and “resolution” for 1/T_0.

Why overlap-save works. In an N -point circular convolution of a length- N block with a length- M filter, the linear result is N + M - 1 long. Its last M-1 samples wrap round onto outputs 0, …, M-2. So exactly the first M-1 outputs are corrupted. The same thing happens in T5 Q4 with M = 2 : only n = 0 is wrong.
Hand shortcut (no DFTs needed). In an exam you do the circular convolutions by hand, not with DFTs:
Overlap-add: the block (length L ) * h (length M ) is exactly N long. So the circular convolution is the ordinary linear convolution. Just convolve.

Overlap-save: linearly convolve the length- N block with h (result N + M - 1 long). Then add the last M-1 samples onto the first M-1. That gives the N -point circular result (this is time aliasing, as in D5).

Resolution = 1/T_0 = F_s/L with L the number of real samples.
Bin spacing = F_s/N with N the DFT length after padding.
Two tones separated by Δ F are resolvable (by the course’s rule) only if Δ F ≥ F_s/L. Zero-padding changes step 2 only.
To fix poor resolution, record longer: L ≥ F_s/Δ F.
Check bin alignment ( k_0 an integer?). If it is aligned and you use a rectangular window, there is no leakage.
If not aligned, a rectangular window gives side lobes at -13 dB falling only slowly (about -18 dB 2 bins away, -26 dB 6 bins away).
If a weak component must be seen near a strong one, use Hanning. Its side lobes are -31 dB and fall fast.
Pay for it in main-lobe width (about 4 bins null to null), so lengthen the record if the tones are close.
Always state the trade-off in your answer: “lower side lobes, wider main lobe”.

Using N instead of L for resolution after zero-padding. Resolution is 1/T_0 = F_s/L. F_s/N is only the bin spacing.
Claiming zero-padding improves resolution. It interpolates the same DTFT. Slide 9’s “better resolution” means a finer grid.
Rounding N down, or forgetting to round to a power of 2 when the question says N = 2^m (T5 Q5: 120 becomes 128, not 64).
Forgetting the mirror bin. A real cosine at k_0 also appears at N - k_0. Bin k > N/2 is a negative frequency, not a frequency above F_s/2.
Calling Hanning “better” without the cost. It lowers side lobes but widens the main lobe (about 2×). Full marks need both halves.
Overlap-save: forgetting the M-1 leading zeros in the first block, or carrying over L samples instead of M-1.
Overlap-save: discarding the last M-1 outputs instead of the first. The wrap-around corrupts the start of each block.
Overlap-add: forgetting to add the overlap, or overlapping by L instead of M-1. Block i starts at n = iL.

Line voltage in a per-phase circuit. For star, V_1 = 415/sqrt3 = 239.6 V. For delta, V_1 = V_L, and the line current is sqrt3 I_1.
Dividing by ω instead of ω_S for torque. τ = P_AG/ω_S. Then P_OUT = τω. Mixing these up gives an error of about s (3–5 %), which loses the mark.
Using R_2' instead of R_2'/s in P_AG, or using R_2'/s for rotor copper loss. Rotor copper loss is 3I_2'^2R_2' = sP_AG (Lecture 7.5.1, “not divided by slip”).
Slip at the wrong speed. The rated speed fixes the pole count. The slip is calculated at the operating speed (1520 rpm in Jun23 c(ii), 1025 rpm in Jun24 c(i)).
Dropping the minus sign in generator mode. s, R_2'/s, P_IN, P_AG and τ are all negative. The course answers keep the signs ( -0.025, -120 Ω, -1451 W, -14.15 Nm).
Adding currents in polar form. I_1 = I_2' + I_M must be done in rectangular form.
Including X_M when told to ignore it (or the reverse). Read each part. In 7.14(a) you ignore it. In 7.14(b) you must not (the course hint says 93.7 A means you forgot it).
Rounding R_2'/s early. 0.2/0.0333 = 6.006 instead of 6.000 is harmless, but s = 0.07 rounded to 0.1 is not. Keep s as an exact fraction.

What it is: a power series in z^-1. The coefficient of z^-n is x(n). So x(3) sits with z^-3, and x(-2) sits with z^+2.
Why it matters for systems: feed x(n)=z^n into an LTI system and the output is y(n)=H(z)z^n with H(z)=Σ_k h(k)z^-k. So H(z) is the z-transform of the impulse response.
Trap: an answer is only complete with its ROC (L07 slide 6). (1)/(1-0.5z^-1) alone does not fix x(n). The pair is “ X(z) + ROC”.
The ROC is the set of z where the sum converges. Convergence depends only on |z|=r, so the ROC is always a ring centred on the origin.

Rotor: either permanent magnets, or a field winding fed with DC field current (excitation) I_F through slip rings. This rotor field is fixed relative to the rotor, so it rotates with the rotor.
1. The core ideas › 1.4 How a synchronous machine works (Lecture 8.1.2, 8.2.2, 8.2.4)

1. The core ideas › 1.4 How a synchronous machine works (Lecture 8.1.2, 8.2.2, 8.2.4)
Turning the excited rotor induces 3ph voltages E_0 in the stator. E_0 is proportional to speed and to I_F (until the iron saturates). Its frequency is set by the speed.

The course defines motoring by the rotor angle: in a motor the stator field leads the rotor, so δ < 0. The course does not use a separate motor equation. You have two equivalent ways to handle a motor:
Course way: keep E_0 = V + jX_S I, but use the generator-convention current, which is the input current reversed: I = -I_in. The answer comes out with δ negative.
Motor convention: take I_m as the current into the machine. Then V = E_0 + jX_S I_m, so E_0 = V - jX_S I_m.
Both give exactly the same E_0. For a motor, “leading pf” means the input current leads V.
Lagging under-excited motor absorbs Q (like an induction motor)
Leading over-excited motor supplies Q to the plant (this is power-factor correction)
One rule that covers both modes: an over-excited synchronous machine generates Q. An under-excited one absorbs Q.

The course uses Q = Ssin(-φ). A lagging current ( φ < 0 ) gives Q > 0. For a load or motor (current in), Q > 0 means it absorbs Q. For a generator (current out), a lagging output current means the generator is delivering Q to the system. Jun23 Q4a confirms this: P = 100 MW and Q = +50 MVAr gives I = 0.7453∠ -26.57^° pu.

δ = 90^° : theoretical stability limit (pull-out). Beyond it, more mechanical input gives less electrical output, so the rotor accelerates away and loses synchronism.
Rated torque is at about δ ≈ 60^° (Lecture 8.2.2). About 75^° is the typical largest operating value, which leaves a safety margin (Lecture 8.4.5).
Losing synchronism causes very large fault currents and oscillating torques, and can damage the generator and turbine (spring-and-disks analogy, 8.4.7).

Lower excitation means a lower P_max. At the same P, an under-excited (leading) generator runs at a larger δ, closer to the limit. That is why the excitation must “not be reduced so far that δ gets close to 90°” (Lecture 8.6.2).

At constant P, plot stator current |I| against I_F. The curve is a “V”:
The minimum |I| is at unity pf (Q = 0), where S = P.
Moving away from that point either way adds |Q|, so S = √(P^2 + Q^2) grows and |I| = S/V grows.
Higher I_F (over-excited): the machine generates Q. Lower I_F (under-excited): it absorbs Q.
A pf-versus- I_F curve is an inverted V with its peak (pf = 1) at the same I_F.
A larger P moves the whole V up and to the right.

Ten of the questions in WS8 and WS9 (WS8 Q1–6, WS9 Q1–4) are pure bias questions. The practice test only covers Weeks 1–5, so there is no past paper evidence for ma
Three facts hold for every FET bias circuit:
I_G ≈ 0 A I_D = I_S so V_R_G = 0 and V_G is set only by what is connected to the gate.
Device Equation Valid range Common trap
JFET (n-channel) I_D = I_DSS(1-(V_GS)/(V_P))^2 V_P ≤ V_GS ≤ 0 Taking the root with V_GS < V_P. A JFET gate must not be forward biased, so V_GS > 0 is also not allowed.
D-MOSFET (n-channel) Same Shockley equation V_GS ≥ V_P. V_GS may be positive (enhancement mode). Stopping the transfer curve at V_GS=0. Then you cannot find a Q-point with I_D > I_DSS.
E-MOSFET (n-channel) I_D = k (V_GS-V_GS(Th))^2, with k = (I_D(on))/((V_GS(on)-V_GS(Th))^2) V_GS > V_GS(Th) ( =V_T ) Using I_DSS, which an E-MOSFET does not have. Find k first.
Quick-sketch points for the Shockley curve (from the Week 7 common-gate example):
For a D-MOSFET, add one point with positive V_GS, for example V_GS=+1 V. In Week 7 Example 1 that gives I_D = 6(1+1/3)^2 = 10.67 mA.
Bias-line (network) equations. These come from KVL around the gate–source loop. Each one is a straight line in the I_D – V_GS plane.
Configuration Bias line Intercepts for plotting
JFET / D-MOSFET fixed bias V_GS = -V_GG (vertical line) none needed
JFET self-bias V_GS = -I_D R_S passes through origin. Pick any I_D for a second point.
Voltage divider (any FET) V_GS = V_G - I_D R_S, with V_G = (R_2 V_DD)/(R_1+R_2) V_GS=V_G at I_D=0. I_D = V_G/R_S at V_GS=0.
Common gate, R_S to -V_SS V_GS = V_SS - I_D R_S same shape as voltage divider, with V_SS in place of V_G
E-MOSFET drain feedback ( R_G from D to G) V_GS = V_DS = V_DD - I_D R_D V_GS=V_DD at I_D=0. I_D = V_DD/R_D at V_GS=0.
Start at WS8 Q3 (750 Ω) and drag R_S: the self-bias line pivots about the origin, and the rejected root always sits to the left of V_P.
V_D = V_DD - I_D R_D V_S = I_D R_S (or -V_SS + I_D R_S) V_DS = V_D - V_S
With a single supply, V_DS = V_DD - I_D(R_D+R_S). With a negative source supply, V_DS = V_DD + V_SS - I_D(R_D+R_S).
Saturation (pinch-off) check. Shockley’s equation and the square law only hold in the saturation region:
JFET / D-MOSFET: V_DS ≥ V_GS - V_P E-MOSFET: V_DS ≥ V_GS - V_GS(Th)
If this check fails, the device is in the ohmic region and your Q-point is wrong. An E-MOSFET with drain feedback always passes, because V_DS = V_GS > V_GS - V_T.

Look at the gate. Is it tied to a battery V_GG through R_G ? That is fixed bias. Is it tied to ground through R_G, with a resistor R_S in the source? That is self-bias, or common gate if the signal enters at the source. Is it fed by R_1 / R_2 ? That is voltage divider. Is R_G connected from drain to gate? That is drain feedback (E-MOSFET).

2. The method › Playbook A: find the Q-point
Mathematical: substitute the bias line into the device equation. Expand into aI_D^2 + bI_D + c = 0. Solve, or use the calculator equation solver. You get two roots.
2. The method › Playbook A: find the Q-point

Choose the valid root. Work out V_GS for each root. For a JFET keep the root with V_P ≤ V_GS ≤ 0. For a D-MOSFET keep the root with V_GS ≥ V_P. For an E-MOSFET keep the root with V_GS > V_GS(Th). The other root always lies on the “mirror” half of the parabola and is not physical.

Sample the analogue impulse response: h(n)=T h_a(nT). With partial fractions this means (A_k)/(s-p_k)longrightarrow(TA_k)/(1-e^p_kTz^-1). Each analogue pole p_k maps to z_k=e^p_kT.
1. The core ideas › 1.7 Impulse invariance (low priority)

Stability is kept ( Re p_k<0⇒|z_k|<1 ). However, the frequency response is a sum of shifted copies of H_a, so it aliases. It is only usable for lowpass and bandpass filters that are well band-limited. This is why slide 17 prefers an Ω_c that beats the stopband spec when impulse invariance is used.

Exam priority: low. At most, expect “state one advantage of the bilinear transform over impulse invariance” (answer: no aliasing).

Monotonic passband. Equiripple stopband. For Ω>Ω_s, Ω_s/Ω<1, so T_N^2(Ω_s/Ω) oscillates between 0 and 1. The stopband gain bounces between 0 (a zero) and its peak value at Ω_s.

Playbook A: Chebyshev ε and N (Type I or II)
If the spec is in Hz: ω = 2π F/F_s. Write ω_p and ω_s as multiples of π.
Pre-warp with T=1 : Ω_i=2tan(ω_i/2). Skip this if the spec is already analogue.
Numerator: cosh^-1 ((√(1-δ_s^2))/(ε δ_s)). Denominator: cosh^-1(Ω_s/Ω_p). Divide, then round up.

Playbook B: Chebyshev I poles and H(s)
β=((√(1+ε^2)+1)/ε)^1/N. Compute the bracket first, then take the N -th root.
φ_k=90^°+(2k+1)(180^°)/(2N) for k=0,…,N-1. All of them lie between 90° and 270°, in the left half-plane.
p_k=r_2cosφ_k+jr_1sinφ_k. Pair the conjugates: (s-p)(s-p^*)=s^2-2 Re(p) s+|p|^2.
K=prod(-p_k) (odd N ), or divide by √(1+ε^2) (even N ). Check |H(jΩ_p)|=δ_p.
For a digital filter, apply the bilinear map (D11).
Playbook C: fill a sample, prove linear phase
Compare the end samples. If h(0)=h(M-1), the filter must be symmetric. If h(0)=-h(M-1), it must be antisymmetric. Fill the gaps by mirroring about α=(M-1)/(2).
If the filter is antisymmetric with odd M, the middle sample is 0.
Write H(ω)=Σ h(n)e^-jω n. Factor out e^-jωα. Pair terms equidistant from α : e^jkω+e^-jkω=2cos kω, e^jkω-e^-jkω=2jsin kω.
Write j=e^jπ/2, so the result is H(ω)=A(ω)e^-j(αω-π/2).
Phase: θ(ω)=-αω (+ π/2 if antisymmetric) when A≥0. Add or subtract π where A<0. Group delay =α.
Name the type and the forced zeros (Table 1.6).
Playbook D: window design by hand
Write h_d(n)=(sin(ω_c n))/(π n), with h_d(0)=ω_c/π. If the question gives a different ideal H_d, do the inverse DTFT integral.
α=(M-1)/(2). Compute h_d(n-α) for n=0,…,M-1. By symmetry you only need about half of them.
Compute w(n) from the course formula, using M-1 in the cosine.
Multiply sample by sample: h(n)=h_d(n-α)w(n). Mark the origin arrow at n=0.
If asked for the response: H(ω)=e^-jαω[h(α)+2Σ_n<alphah(n)cos((α-n)ω)]. Evaluate at ω=0, ω_c and π.

How to use this: sit it timed first (120 min, open book). Do not open this until time is up.

The paper is “Resources/eec jun24 exam.pdf” (Electric Energy Conversion, Semester 1 2024, W.L. Soong). The course gives numerical answers only (“eec jun24 exam numerical answers”). This pack is the full solution set. Every number below was recomputed in Python and checked against those answers. Where my value differs in the last digit, the note says why.

Marking: each part’s total is the official one from the paper’s cover table. The split inside a part (“1 mark for …”) is my suggested allocation, built the way a marker usually awards method and answer marks. Be strict: give yourself a mark only if your script shows the line that earns it.
Figures: the paper’s own figures are reproduced under each question. They confirm the values used below:
Q1c: series R = 100 Ω and jX_L = j40 Ω (the same values that the official answers give: P = 400 W and Q = 160 VAr at 2 A).
Q1d: a series RL load with the capacitor C across the supply.
Q2b: a 15 Ω series resistor, then a 6:1 ideal transformer, then a 0.3 Ω load.
Q3a: three torque–speed curves. Top to bottom they are synchronous, DC and induction, as the answer sheet says.
All phasors are rms. φ is the angle of the current relative to the voltage, so lagging means φ < 0.
Time. 120 min for 80 marks is 1.5 min per mark. Budget about 28 min per question and keep 8 min spare. Write the budget for each part next to it in the first minute (for example, 3c [10] = 15 min).
Order of attack. Every question is 20 marks, so start where you are fastest.
Q1 (Ch1–2) and Q2 (Ch3) first. They are the most practised material, from the quiz and test. Bank about 35 of the 40 marks in 55 min.
Q3 next. 3b and 3c are plug-in induction-machine calculations. 3c alone is 10 marks.
Q4 last. 4a and 4b are short per-unit phasor sums. Do not leave 4c (9 marks) to the final 3 minutes. Words-only answers earn marks quickly, about one solid point per mark.
Paper-specific habits that earn marks here.

Three-phase means per-phase. Q1b, Q2c, Q3b, Q3c and Q4a all have line values. Divide the line voltage by sqrt3 (star), and divide three-phase power by 3, before you use any per-phase formula. Write “assume star” if the question does not say.
Signs carry marks. Q_C < 0 in Q1d. s, R_2'/s, P_IN, P_AG and τ are all negative in Q3c (generator). Leading means +cos^-1 pf in Q4b.
Read which value the part uses. Q1c(ii) and Q1d(iii) each give new data. Do not carry over the earlier current or Q_C.
Units asked for. Q4a(i) asks for X_S in per-unit, not ohms. Q1d(iii) asks for capacitance in μF.
Words only in Q4c. No sketches or equations. Name the effect, the circuit element that models it, and how it varies.

Open book. Tab your notes at: back-emf equation and F = B^2A/2µ_0 (Ch3), the induction equivalent circuit and power flow (Ch7), and E_0 = V + jX_SI and P = VE_0sinδ/X_S (Ch8). Do not spend exam time reading theory. Look up a formula, then go.

Each phase is a pair of opposite coils. The three magnetic axes are 120° apart. Positive current gives a field along the axis and negative current reverses it. This gives 6 field directions, which step round to make a stepwise rotating field (stepper motor, not examinable).
Balanced 3ph currents give a field of constant magnitude rotating at constant speed n_S.
Phase sequence sets the direction: abc = bca = cab one way, acb = cba = bac the other. Swapping any two supply leads reverses rotation. A cyclic relabelling of all three does not.
One electrical cycle moves the field one pole-pair, which is 1/p of a revolution. Hence n_S = 60f/p.
A single-phase winding gives a pulsating field (forward plus backward rotating), so the starting torque is zero. It needs an auxiliary winding and capacitor to start (not examinable).

Transmission system (9.1.3): drawn as a single-line diagram (one line represents 3ph). A busbar is a node where every point is at the same (nominal) voltage. Generators and lines are paralleled for reliability (one can fail), maintenance without interrupting supply, and running the most efficient number of generators for the demand.

Ch1–2 (Q1, and Q4c has asked these)

Real, reactive, apparent power (Jun24 4c(i)): P comes from the current in phase with V; it is the average of instantaneous power, net energy to the load, does useful work, absorbed by resistors. Q comes from the quadrature current; energy oscillates between source and load with zero mean; inductors absorb it, capacitors generate it; no useful work but needs

PFC (Jun23 4c(i)): loads (mainly induction motors) draw Q, which is energy oscillating in the system. It loads generators, transformers and lines and adds losses. A parallel capacitor (or over-excited sync motor) generates Q locally, so the supply Q, S and current fall. P and the load are unchanged. Tariffs on VA make it pay.
Why three-phase: a balanced 3ph winding makes a constant rotating field, so machines self-start; total instantaneous power is constant (smooth, quiet); better use of material and conductors.
Why efficiency matters: limited stored energy (EVs), running cost over the life, and heat removal limits the rating.
Ch3 (Q2, quiz and test last questions)

Choosing primary turns (2023 quiz Q7): the back-emf equation links turns and peak flux for a given V and f; choose turns so B is just below saturation. Too few: B too high, saturation, high and distorted current, overheating. Too many: low B, more winding R, more copper loss, lower η, possible overheating.

Ideal vs real, load R doubled (2024 test Q8): ideal: V set only by input V and turns ratio, so unchanged; current halves (Ohm’s law). Real: series R and leakage X drop less voltage at lower current, so V rises slightly; current falls to slightly more than half.

Transformer losses (Jun24 4c(ii)): copper loss: I^2R heating of the windings, series winding R, varies with the square of output. Iron loss: hysteresis (domain reversal) and eddy currents (induced core currents), core-loss resistance in the shunt branch, constant with load (set by V and f). Max η where they are equal.
V_2' phase, resistive load (Jun23 2c(iii)): lags, because the series reactance makes the current lag V_1 and the load voltage is in phase with the current.
OC voltage halved (Jun24 2c(iii)): fixed shunt impedance: current ×0.5, P and Q ×0.25, pf ×1. A real core draws even less current (further below the knee).

Transformer no-load current not zero: magnetising current (finite permeability, X_M, lags 90°) plus core-loss current (hysteresis and eddy, R_C, in phase). Saturation makes it large and distorted at high V.

Airgap effect: μr = 1, so even a short gap dominates the reluctance; L falls, more current for the same flux, but L becomes linear; most energy and the force are in the gap; in an IM the gap is unavoidable, so it is kept small (magnetising current, pf).
Laminations and silicon steel: thin insulated laminations break eddy-current paths; silicon raises resistivity and lowers hysteresis loss.

IM no-load current not zero (Jun24 4c(iii)): magnetising current sets up the airgap flux, and is large because of the airgap ( X_M ). A core-loss component covers hysteresis and eddy currents ( R_C ). Friction (bearings) and windage (air, fan) need a little power, so there is a small slip and rotor current. The pf is low.
Perfectly conducting rotor, R_2' = 0 (Jun23 4c(iii)): no rotor loss, so higher efficiency. s_τmax = 0, so the curve is vertical at n_S, like a synchronous machine. Zero starting torque.

Transformer vs IM (Jun23 4c(ii)): both have primary and secondary windings on a magnetic core, both run on 3ph AC, with similar circuits. The IM secondary rotates and is short-circuited, the rotor frequency is sf, the rotor R is divided by s, and the airgap makes the magnetising current much larger.
Torque production: rotating field at n_S ; slip induces slip-frequency emf in the shorted rotor; rotor currents in the field give force; at n_S no change of flux, so no emf, current or torque.

V/f control: frequency sets n_S ; flux ∝ V/f ; reducing f alone saturates the core (large current); keeping V/f constant keeps flux and τ_max, so the curve slides along the speed axis; small boost at low f for the R_1 drop.
Tests: DC test gives R_1 ; no-load (s ≈ 0) gives R_C, X_M (includes friction and windage); blocked rotor (s = 1, low V) gives R_1 + R_2' and X; split X equally.
Wound rotor and external R: raises s_τmax and starting torque, lowers starting current, τ_max unchanged; extra rotor loss, so cut it out at speed.
IM as generator: driven above n_S, s < 0, R_2'/s negative, power reverses; still absorbs Q for magnetising; cannot control its own Q or voltage; suits wind and regenerative braking.
Sync machine advantages: exact speed, high efficiency, and controllable Q (unlike an IM).

Induction vs synchronous: sync runs exactly at n_S, IM below it with slip rising with load; sync rotor field from DC or magnets, IM rotor currents induced; IM always absorbs Q (lagging), sync Q set by field current; IM self-starting, cheap, robust.

Industrial pf lagging, why sync motors: plants are mostly induction motors, which absorb Q; VA tariffs and cable loading; an over-excited sync motor generates Q while driving its load; limited to √(S^2 - P^2).

Field current on an infinite bus: V and f fixed by the system; P set by the turbine; I_F sets E_0 and Q; over-excited delivers Q (lagging), under-excited absorbs Q (leading, larger δ, less stable); V-curve minimum at unity pf.
Q capability limit: stator current heating ( S_rated, so Q = √(S^2 - P^2) ), rotor field heating on the over-excited side, stability (δ → 90°) on the under-excited side.

Per-unit advantages: values relative to rating show size at a glance; similar machines have similar pu values (easy error check); no √3 or 3, line = phase; transformer impedances the same on both sides.
Salient vs round rotor: low speed (hydro) needs many poles, easy with salient poles, low stress; high speed (2–4 poles, 3000 rpm) needs a strong round rotor with slotted winding, low windage.
Not self-starting: at standstill the field sweeps past and the torque alternates each half cycle, average zero; start with a pony motor, damper (starting) cage or an inverter ramp.

Sync vs DC circuit: both an emf proportional to speed and field behind a series impedance; DC uses R and DC quantities; sync uses mainly X_S and phasors, where δ controls P and lvert E_0rvert controls Q.
High-voltage transmission: same power, current ∝ 1/V ; loss ∝ I^2, so loss falls with V^2 ; thinner conductors, less voltage drop; transformers make stepping cheap.
Paralleled lines and generators: reliability (fault tolerance), maintenance without interrupting supply, run the most efficient number of generators.
Renewables: unlimited resource, zero operating emissions; but economic (cost, subsidies), technical (variability, storms) and environmental (visual, noise) difficulties.
Fossil fuels: finite reserves; CO₂ (global warming), SOₓ and NOₓ (acid rain); nuclear has radioactive waste.

P1. Sample a CT signal; find T_s and samples (ST1 Q1a, T1 Q2)
T_s = 1/F_s. List every F_0 : divide the t coefficient by 2π ( sin(480π t) is 240 Hz). Nyquist rate = 2F_max.
Substitute t = nT_s : each term becomes ω_0 = 2π F_0/F_s.
Reduce each ω_0 into (-π, π] ; use cos(2π kn) = 1, cos(π n) = (-1)^n.
Tidy negative frequencies ( sin flips sign) and combine like terms.
Evaluate the requested samples after reducing. Say whether aliasing occurred ( F_0 vs F_s/2 ).
Ideal DAC, if asked: y(t) = x(n)rvert_n = F_st with the reduced ω.
DT: for each component f_i = ω_i/2π. Any irrational f_i (leftover π ): aperiodic, stop.
Write f_i = k_i/N_i in lowest terms; N = LCM(N_i). Products: same rule (both factors must be periodic).
Check: T1 Q1(e) f = 14, 116, 18 : N = 16. Reference self-test: cos(3π n/7) + sin(π n/4) : N = LCM(14, 8) = 56.

Check: ST1 Q1(b) x(n) = 2, undersetuparrow1, 0.5, 0, 1, n = -1..3 (note x(2) = 0 ).
P5. Sequence operations and energy (ST1 Q2)
Write the index under every sample (ST1: x(0) = 1, the underlined third sample, so n = -2..3 ).
Shifts: add the delay to every index; for sums, one row per copy, add columns.
Upsample x(n/2) : index m → 2m, zeros between. Downsample x(2n) : keep even indices, halve them.
(-1)^n : negate odd-index samples (check the index, not the position in the list).
x(α n + β) : substitute each n directly.

P6. System properties, tick boxes (ST1 Q3, T2 Q1, T3 Q1)
Static? Any index other than n, any sum, any y(n-k) : dynamic.
Linear? x = 0 ⇒ y = 0 ? A constant term or x^2, lvert xrvert, cos x fails. n -dependent gains are fine.
TI? Two columns: (i) replace x(·) by x(· - d), leave explicit n ; (ii) replace every n by n - d. Compare. Explicit n coefficient, u[n] factor, x(2n), x(-n) : time-varying.
Causal? Any x(n+k), k>0, at any n (check negative n for x(-n) ).
Stable? Bound lvert yrvert by M_x, or use x = u(n) to blow it up.
Write a two-word reason beside every tick.

Hz from the argument. sin(480π t) is 240 Hz: divide by 2π.

“Looks linear”. y = 1 + 2x and x[n+1] - 1 fail x = 0 ⇒ y = 0 ; nx(n), x(2n) are linear (only time-varying).
Causality at negative n. x(-n) and x(-n+2) use future inputs for n < 0 (or n ≤ 0 ).
Correlation convention. Lecture r_xy(l) and tutorial R_xy(l) are lag-reversed; T3 Q7’s list read with the lecture definition is backwards. State yours.
Modes from the x side. Only y coefficients enter; no feedback means no modes (say so).
Recursion sign flip. y(n) - y(n-1) + y(n-2) becomes y(n) = y(n-1) - y(n-2) + …
ICs into the closed form. Fit constants at y(0), y(1) from recursion, never at y(-1), y(-2) (T3 Q4: y(0) = 1 - (-1) - 14(2) = 1.5 ).
Repeated root. Needs nλ^n ; for λ = 1 the modes are 1 and n.
m ≥ k in h(n). The mode form starts late; add δ terms.
Geometric off by one. Σ_0^n has n + 1 terms; a = b gives (n+1)a^n, not 0/0.
No range on a convolution. Attach u(n) or the piecewise ranges; finite windows need several cases.
“Marginally stable” is unstable for BIBO: lvertλrvert = 1, u(n), (n+1)u(n), cos(ω_0n)u(n) are not absolutely summable (ST1 Q4).
ST1 Q4(d) uses the given h, (2^-n + 3^-n)u(n), not the answer to (c).
Input phase. cos(ω n + φ) gives lvert Hrvertcos(ω n + φ + θ) ; both phases appear. DC is multiplied by H(0), not 1.
Negative real H. Magnitude is positive; add ±π to the phase (T4 Q4).
H(ω) needs stability. H(z) at z = e^jω only if the ROC contains the unit circle.
Linear via DFT. N ≥ L + M - 1, not max(L, M) or L + M.
Resolution. Zero padding gives a finer grid, not resolution. Δ F = F_s/L ; round N up to 2^m (T5 Q5: 120 becomes 128).
Circular index. All DFT shifts and reversals are mod N : x((-n))_N = x(N - n), not x(-n).
No ROC. X(z) without its ROC is half an answer. a^nu(n) and -a^nu(-n-1) have the same X(z).
Reversal ROC. x(-n) inverts and swaps the radii (T6 Q1d: 13 < lvert zrvert < 2 becomes 12 < lvert zrvert < 3 ).
Anti-causal sign. (A)/(1 - pz^-1), lvert zrvert < lvert prvert gives -Ap^nu(-n-1), not Ap^nu(-n).
Non-monic factors. (3 - z^-1) must become 3(1 - 13z^-1) before cover-up (T7 Q1).
Improper fraction. Equal z^-1 degrees give a Kδ(n) term; K is the ratio of the highest-power coefficients (T8 Q5: 0.64/(-1.2) = -0.5333 ).
Causal vs inside the circle. Each term’s causality comes from the pole’s position relative to the ROC; the unit circle only decides which ROC is stable.
Unilateral shift. y(n-2) → z^-2Y + z^-1y(-1) + y(-2) : three terms. No IC terms for a causal input.
Hz vs rad/sample. ω = 2π F/F_s for digital; Ω = 2π F only for a pure analogue question (T9 Q6).
Notch normalisation. Normalise where the question says (T8 Q3: ω = π, z^-1 = -1 ).
Zero on the circle. Notch and comb filters have no stable inverse. Zeros on the circle are not “minimum phase”.
No prewarp. Using ω/T or 2π F in a bilinear design moves the edges.
δ_p meaning. In this course δ_p is the minimum passband gain 10^-A_p/20 (0.8913 for 1 dB), not 1 - 10^-A_p/20.
cos^-1 in Chebyshev N. Use cosh^-1 ; the arguments exceed 1.
Which Ω_c. Butterworth passband-exact and stopband-exact Ω_c differ (T9 Q5: 0.8140 vs 1.2799). State your choice.
Window index. Use M - 1 in the cosine and shift h_d(n - α). Course Hanning, M = 5 : 0, 0.5, 1, 0.5, 0.

Pick the form. I_S, n, I_D given: V_D = nV_T(I_D/I_S). V_D given: full Shockley. Change in current: Δ V_D = nV_T(I_2/I_1), showing that I_S cancels. Two points: divide for n, back-substitute for I_S, check with the other point.
Say “ I_D I_S, so the −1 is negligible”.
Temperature: I_S×2^Δ T/10 ; V_D falls 2.5 mV/°C.
Procedure 4: diode circuit, assume and verify (PT Q3, WS3 Q15–Q17)
Model. Write the one named: 1st (ideal), 2nd ( V_D ), 3rd ( V_D + r_D ).
Guess each state and write it (“D1 ON, D2 OFF”). Anode nearer the more positive source: probably ON.

Redraw and solve. ON diodes become their model branch, OFF diodes open. Find i_d (anode → cathode) for each ON diode and v_d = V_anode - V_cathode for each OFF diode. An OFF branch carries no current, so its resistors drop nothing but its batteries still count. Thévenin the rest of the circuit if there is one diode.
Verify. ON needs i_d > 0 ; OFF needs v_d < V_D (ideal: < 0 ). If a check fails, flip that diode and repeat. Write the sentence: “ I = 15.3 µA > 0, so all three conduct.”
Only then compute V_o. For several ON diodes feeding one node, add KCL as the third equation.
Procedure 5: rectifier with a capacitor filter (WS3 Q9, Q14, Q20–21)
V_m = sqrt2V_s(rms) (centre tap: half-winding). V_P = V_m - V_D or V_m - 2V_D (bridge).
Write “half-wave” or “full-wave”. V_r = V_P/(fCR) or V_P/(2fCR) ; rearrange for C when designing. If a ripple factor is given, convert: V_r(pp) = 2sqrt3 rV_dc.
ωΔ t = √(2V_r/V_P) rad; fraction ωΔ t/2π.
i_Dav, i_Dmax (formula-sheet half-wave forms; full-wave forms in the filter table).
PIV (half-wave with C: 2V_m ), output frequency, diode rating ≥ 1.5× PIV.
Procedure 6: Zener regulator (PT Q4, WS3 Q10, Q13, Q22)
Analysis: assume breakdown. Ideal: V_O = V_Z, I_S = (V_s - V_Z)/R_S, I_L = V_Z/R_L, I_Z = I_S - I_L. With r_z : the single nodal equation for V_O.
Check I_Z > 0. If not, the Zener is off and V_O = V_sR_L/(R_L + R_S).
Design: V_Z = V_L. Size R_S at lowest supply and heaviest load: R_S = (V_s,min - V_Z)/(I_L,max + I_Z,min).
Check the other extreme (highest supply, no load): I_Z,max and P_Z,max = V_ZI_Z,max. That is often the last mark.
Load range: R_L,min from I_R,min - I_Z,min ; R_L,max from I_R,max - I_Z,max ( ∞ if ≤ 0 ).
Procedure 7: clipper or clamper (PT Q5, WS3 Q11–Q12, Q18)
Mark where v_o is taken and trace the only direction current can flow through each diode.
Assume OFF; write v_d in terms of v_i ; set v_d = V_D (or 0): v_iT.
One linear equation for v_o per region (KVL with battery signs as you meet them).
Square wave: evaluate both levels. Sine: find the crossing of v_iT.
Sketch v_o under v_i, same time axis, levels labelled; or draw the transfer characteristic (one line per state, meeting at v_iT ).
Clamper: find the half-cycle that charges C ( V_C = peak -V_D ); in the other half v_o = v_i ± V_C ; check that peak-to-peak is unchanged.
Procedure 8: BJT DC bias with the state given (assume active) (PT Q6–Q7, WS5 Q3–Q9)
Thévenin the base (Procedure 1) if two resistors or two supplies meet there. For a divider, first write “ β R_E = …, 10R_2 = …, so the approximation is / is not valid”.
Redraw with the active model (0.7 V B–E, β I_B C→E). A “redraw” part earns marks for every labelled element.
Base loop with I_E = (β+1)I_B : I_B = (V_Th - 0.7)/(R_Th + (β+1)R_E). Approximate divider: I_E = (V_B - 0.7)/R_E.
Output loop: V_CE = V_CC - I_CR_C - I_ER_E ; node voltages V_E, V_C, V_B.
Check: “ I_B > 0 and V_CE = … > 0.2 V, so active.” If V_CE is negative, go to Procedure 9 step 5.
Procedure 9: BJT state unknown (guess, analyse, check) (WS5 Q9–Q15)
Simplify: Thévenin the base, and the collector if it has two supplies.
Guess: EBJ clearly forward biased → active; base undriven or reverse biased → cut-off.
Analyse with that model: active needs I_B, V_CE ; saturation needs I_B, I_C ; cut-off needs V_BE.
Check: active I_B > 0, lvert V_CErvert > 0.2 ; saturation I_B, I_C > 0, I_C < β I_B ; cut-off lvert V_BErvert < 0.7.
Redirect: V_CE ≤ 0.2 → saturation ( V_CE = 0.2, solve base and collector loops with I_E = I_B + I_C ); I_B ≤ 0 → cut-off.
Quote the forced β ( I_C/I_B ) for saturation.
Procedure 10: β range or guaranteed saturation (WS5 Q12–Q13, Q16)
Write V_CE (or I_C ) as a function of β with the active model.
“Stays active for all β”: impose V_CE ≥ 0.2 at β_max.
“Always saturated”: at the edge, I_C = β I_B and V_CE = 0.2, at β_min.
Solve the inequality for the unknown; state which β is the worst case and why. A negative resistance means “no value works”: say so.
Range given: compute and quote both ends.
Procedure 11: load line and Q-point on printed characteristics (PT Q6)
V_CE = V_CC - I_C(R_C + R_E) ; intercepts V_CC and V_CC/(R_C + R_E) ; rule the line.
Q where the line meets I_BQ (interpolate between printed curves).
Write the I_CQ and V_CEQ you read, then β_dc = I_CQ/I_BQ from your readings. Quote the analytical values as a cross-check.
Procedure 12: bias design (WS5 Q4–Q6, Q17–Q19, Lecture 4)
List the targets; a stated V_CE > 0.2 V means active.
Currents first: I_B = I_C/β, I_E = I_C/α.
Each resistor R = V_R/I_R, starting with the loop that has one unknown. Divider: rules in the state/design table, and say whether the base current was neglected.
Standard values, then re-analyse (exact method) and quote the % error.
Procedure 13: two-BJT DC circuits (PT Q8, WS6 Q12–Q17)
Draw real current arrows on every BJT (pnp: I_B, I_C out, I_E in).
Start with the transistor whose base loop is self-contained, or with a diode-connected BJT (fixes a level one V_BE away).
Carry the shared node into the next stage; include I_B2 in the node KCL if accuracy matters, and say whether you did.
Use each transistor’s own β; a β that only sets a level never appears in the answer.

AC equivalent: V_CC to ground, capacitors shorted, shorted resistors deleted, model inserted.

Name the configuration: in at base → CE or follower; in at emitter → CB; out at collector → CE/CB; out at emitter → follower; R_F from collector to base → collector feedback. Mark what is in the emitter at AC: 0, R_E, R_E1 or R_E∥ R_L.

v_out = -β i_b × (everything from collector to AC ground, including the next stage’s r_π ).
Divide; simplify only at the end; check that it collapses to the standard result when the extra resistors go to 0 or ∞.

g_m from the g_m table with the right formula for the device. r_d = 1/g_os, or ∞ if not given (say so).
